item.title: When Your Child's Meltdown Means You're Winning
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Child's Meltdown Means You're Winning

A bigger blowup after you change your response is a test of the old pattern.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • When you change your response to a reactive pattern, it often escalates before it fades.
  • The boundaries that get tested hardest are the ones that used to bend sometimes.
  • Giving in on the bigger, second blowup teaches a lesson that the old strategy still works.

Parents tell me this all the time, usually with panic and a little betrayal in their voice: "I finally changed how I respond, and it got worse." Early in my career, when I would hear this, I would sheepishly shrink down in my office chair. After all, these parents did everything right, and their kid blew up bigger than ever. But over the years, I realized that's not proof that the new approach failed. In fact, most of the time, it's proof that it's finally working. I have seen this exact sequence more times than I can count in 35 years of clinical work: the moment a parent stops feeding an old reactive pattern, the pattern doesn't quietly retire. It fights back first, harder than it's ever fought before.

The Blowup Right Before the Breakthrough

Psychologists call this an extinction burst: a temporary spike in a behavior right after it stops getting the response that used to work. Your child's nervous system isn't losing. The old pattern is throwing everything it's got at you, one last time, because it's never had to try this hard before. By the way, this dogged determination to frantically try to get what you want gets played out at casinos across the land. Just think about all those people at the slot machines who pour in a big chunk of money before they finally give up.

It was surprising to me, even after decades of watching this occur, how predictable the size of the burst is. The boundaries that get tested hardest aren't the strict ones. They're the inconsistent ones, the "no" that occasionally caved if the tantrum ran long enough. If you'll indulge me in taking you back to the casino for a moment, a slot machine is harder to walk away from than a vending machine. The reason is that the slot machine has likely paid out before. An inconsistent limit teaches a nervous system that persistence works. It just never says exactly when.

The Example of Elaine and Ben

I worked with a mother, Elaine (fictitious names here to protect privacy), who'd finally stopped negotiating bedtime with her 7-year-old son, Ben, after months of nightly haggling. Elaine was pumped up that for night one, there was some mild protest. She then became discouraged that for night two, she witnessed Ben having a full-blown, thrashing meltdown bigger than anything she'd seen in a year. She nearly went back to negotiating, but thankfully, she didn't. Then, for night three, there was nothing in terms of Ben's reactivity. The system had made its last, loudest bid, and once it didn't pay off, it stopped bidding.

You might find it surprising that many reactive children have told me things that bluntly confirm this. One 13-year-old put it plainly: "Dude, I mean, Dr. Jeff, like, I'm a drama queen. I kept going on and on with my parents because it worked before." She wasn't escalating for the thrill of it; she was running a strategy with a track record. By the way, many other kids have confided in me how they "worked their parents by freaking out."

Giving in Now Costs More Than It Ever Did

This is the exact moment most parents quietly undo their own progress, and it's the whole subject of a chapter in my book, 24 Hours to a Less Reactive Child, because the timing of the mistake matters more than the mistake itself. Caving on the bigger, second blowup doesn't just erase the last few days of work. It teaches something worse than never changing anything: The old strategy still works; it just needs more volume now. The bar for "enough" just went up.

None of this applies to real danger. A child hurting themselves or someone else calls for safety and professional support, not patience. But an ordinary blowup that's louder than usual, right after you've changed something? That's not a step backward; it's the last, loudest argument an old pattern has left to make.

The Takeaway

The next flare-up that's bigger than the last one isn't a verdict on your new approach. It's the closest thing to validation you're going to get, as long as you hold your mud.

item.title: The Weaponization of Labels
item.description:
Persuasion

The Weaponization of Labels

How labels influence what we see.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • From Nazi propaganda to political rhetoric, dehumanizing labels make it easier to dismiss or harm "others."
  • Nobel-winning science was nearly buried by labels.
  • Counter labels by asking what they describe, and separate the claim from the person.

I am increasingly concerned about how labels are being weaponized and the polarizing effects they are having on us. Let’s take a look at how labels can influence us.

What Is a Label?

A label is a word or phrase that is attached to a person, group, idea, or thing to put it into a category. Labels are lenses that influence how we see things and how we interpret our world.

Our brains are wired to categorize or sort things into groups so we can make quick decisions without having to re-analyze every situation. Labels help us organize knowledge and predict what to expect from a person or an idea.

Benefits and Harms

Labels can help us or harm us.

For example, a medical diagnosis is a label. A diagnosis tells a doctor what treatment options exist, but can also limit a doctor’s beliefs about how effective treatments may be.

Another label is "scientifically supported," which can help people separate reliable information from unproven claims, or it can cause people to distrust information because they have learned how heavily science has been influenced by large industries, such as the tobacco and pharmaceutical industries.

Labels can be helpful or harmful.
Source: AI-Generated, Google Gemini

Labels can lead to stigma, which is built upon a series of steps: People label a difference, attach a stereotype to it, separate "us" from "them," and then discriminate against the “others.”

In a study published in Science, healthy volunteers were labeled with a psychiatric diagnosis. The staff then interpreted their entirely normal behavior through the lens of that label. The label didn't just identify them with their diagnosis. It changed the way the staff judged their behavior.

A label is never just information. It is always a lens, and lenses can be applied by people who want us to see things in a particular way.

The Weaponization of Labels

Because labels shape perception so powerfully, they're one of the strongest tools of manipulation. A label used to shut down thought, rather than inform it, has been weaponized.

The Military

Military labels
Source: AI-Generated, Google Gemini

It's difficult for ordinary people to harm others if they see them as fully human. Militaries remove that barrier by comparing the enemy to animals, or reducing them to cold, unfeeling objects.

Both of these methods strip away the qualities that cause us to see others as human. Nazi Germany described Jewish people as “vermin.” Rwandan radio called Tutsis "cockroaches" during the 1994 genocide. WWII propaganda portrayed Japanese soldiers as subhuman. Once a group is viewed as less than human, harming them becomes easier.

article continues after advertisement
Political labels
Source: AI-Generated, Google Gemini

Politics

Politics runs on labels, which are used to discredit opponents. Research has found that Americans across the spectrum increasingly describe the opposing party in less-than-human terms. A label like "extremist" is often employed in an effort to stop people from viewing the others’ opinions as worthy of consideration.

Science and Medicine

This same tactic now exists in science. Labels like "quack" or "pseudoscience" can end a scientific conversation before the evidence is even evaluated.

Scientific labels
Source: AI-Generated, Google Gemini

Consider two Nobel Prize–winning discoveries that were initially dismissed. When Australian scientists Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed that a bacterium caused most stomach ulcers, their work was rejected by conference organizers and delayed by skeptical reviewers, because it contradicted the dominant narrative of the time. They were right, and won the 2005 Nobel Prize. Stanley Prusiner's idea that a misfolded protein could cause neurodegenerative disease was met with public ridicule. Later, scientists who rejected the idea that prions could cause neurodegenerative disorders were labeled "prion heretics." Prusiner won the Nobel Prize.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, labels such as “Anti-vaxxer,” “Fear porn addict,” “Misinformation spreader,” “Radical left,” “MAGA extremist, "Quack," “Denier, and ”Conspiracy theorist” were used in an attempt to sway public opinion.

The Risks of Weaponizing Labels

Weaponizing labels in science and medicine can lead to disastrous results.

Medical breakthroughs can be buried. If Marshall, Warren, or Prusiner had been effectively discredited by a label, it may have taken many more decades to understand the cause of ulcers or neurodegenerative disorders. Unconventional ideas need testing, not dismissal.

Legitimate treatments can be suppressed. An unfamiliar treatment can be labeled dangerous or fraudulent before it's fully evaluated. This can result in the death of patients who are denied access to novel treatments.

article continues after advertisement

Financial interests can distort which treatments are labeled as legitimate therapies. A review of thousands of studies found industry-sponsored research is more likely to report favorable results than independently funded research. When a company owns an expensive treatment, there's an incentive to cast doubt on cheaper alternatives.

This doesn't mean every unconventional claim is a suppressed truth. Many fringe claims are fringe because the evidence doesn't support them, and some skepticism is essential to science. The danger is substituting a label for a legitimate evaluation.

Self-stigma Labels
Source: AI-Generated, Google Gemini

The Psychology of Being Labeled

Labels change how we see ourselves, not just how others see us. Psychologists call this “self-stigma.” This process involves internalizing a hostile label that can damage our self-esteem and increase our shame. Being on the receiving end of a weaponized label can produce anxiety, isolation, and a sense of being judged.

Dealing With Weaponized Labels

How can we deal with weaponized labels? Here are some options:

  • Ask what the label describes, not just what it implies. It should point toward evidence, not replace it.
  • Separate the claim from the person. Judge an idea on its merits, not the person who holds it.
  • Notice emotional versus informational words. If a word triggers contempt rather than curiosity, pause rather than rushing to judgment.
  • Ask who benefits if you accept a label without question.
  • Apply the scrutiny you'd want applied to your own beliefs. Dismissing an argument with a label is easy. Engaging it is harder, and more honest.
article continues after advertisement

Labels will always be part of how we think. The goal isn't to eliminate them but, rather, to notice when they stop helping us understand the world and start causing us to view it through a polarized lens that divides rather than unites us.

item.title: On Childhood Trauma, Growth, and Being the Author of Your Story
item.description:
Cognitive Reappraisal

On Childhood Trauma, Growth, and Being the Author of Your Story

The past cannot be changed—but the meaning we assign to it can.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Good teaching does not end questions; it multiplies them. Enter with three, leave with 10.
  • Reappraisal never calls abuse or neglect "wonderful." What can become wonderful is having endured and grown.
  • Reframing a painful past is a choice survivors make in their own time—never a demand others may place on them.

It was my first day as a Ph.D. student—and my first day, ever, of teaching. I had prepared the lecture carefully, printed handouts, and rehearsed my opening lines. As I left my office and walked toward the elevator, my mentor passed by and asked where I was headed. "I'm teaching," I said.

He replied, casually, without slowing down: "Don't teach them. Confuse them."

It took me perhaps 10 years to understand what he meant. My job as a teacher, he was telling me, is not to answer questions and deliver certainty. It is to trigger questions and wondering. I eventually turned his advice into my measure of a good class: If students enter with three questions and leave with 10, I have done my job.

And so, in his honor, let me try to confuse you.

The Most Confusing Sentence I Know

There is a sentence I share with my students—a cousin of an old line often attributed to the novelist Tom Robbins, sharpened for my purposes—that reliably confuses every classroom it enters:

It is never too late to decide that you have had a wonderful childhood.

The first objection arrives immediately: Childhood is fixed. It was what it was. How can an adult retroactively change it and conclude it was wonderful?

Then comes the harder objection, and my students are right to raise it: What about the person who endured sexual abuse as a child? Psychological neglect? Physical violence? All three? How could anyone—why should anyone—call that childhood wonderful?

What the Sentence Does Not Mean

Let me be absolutely clear, because everything depends on this. Nothing about abuse, neglect, or violence is wonderful. Nothing. No reframe softens what was done, and no reframe excuses the person who did it. The sentence is also never a demand: No one may hand it to a survivor as an assignment. For many, grief, anger, and the pursuit of justice must come first—and the timing of any reframing belongs to the survivor alone, often best undertaken with professional support.

What the sentence points to is something else entirely. The wonder is not in what happened. The wonder is in the person it happened to: that they endured it; that they survived what no child should face; that they carried it and still grew. Being a victim of violence is a fact of a person's history—but it cannot define who they are, and it does not get to determine who they become. Imagine facing a hard challenge as an adult while knowing, deep in your bones: I faced a thousand times worse as a child, and I did not break. That knowledge is wonderful. That is what the sentence means.

This connects to one way of understanding psychotherapy's deeper aim: the cultivation of multiperspectivity—the capacity to view one's situation from more than one vantage point. When that capacity grows, something important often shifts: The blame and guilt a child wrongly carried—"It must have been my fault"—move to where they always belonged, with those who were responsible. The facts do not change. The meaning, and the verdict on the self, can.

The Science of the Second Look

Modern psychology has a name for this: cognitive reappraisal—changing an emotion by changing the interpretation of the situation that produced it (Gross, 1998). A large meta-analysis of emotion-regulation strategies found reappraisal to be among the most consistently effective for modifying emotional experience (Webb, Miles, & Sheeran, 2012). Powerful, however, is not limitless: Some wounds require treatment, justice, or simply time before meaning can begin to shift. It may be one of the most reliable psychological tools we possess: The facts stay fixed, and the feeling still moves.

Research on narrative identity points the same way from a different angle. Well-being tracks not only what happened to us but also the stories we construct about it—and people who narrate hard chapters with themes of redemption, growth, and agency tend to report greater well-being than those whose stories end where the harm ended (McAdams & McLean, 2013). Many survivors of severe adversity, though by no means all, also report experiencing growth in its aftermath—deepened relationships, changed priorities, a sense of strength (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 2004). Researchers continue to examine how much of this reported growth reflects deep psychological change and how much reflects the meaning people need to construct—but even that act of construction may itself matter. None of this makes the adversity good. It makes the person's response to it consequential.

Twenty-Seven Years

Consider the most famous demonstration in living memory. A young lawyer who fought an unjust system spent 27 years in prison. He emerged with every conceivable justification for rage—and called instead for reconciliation between Black and white South Africans, becoming his country's president and one of history's enduring images of moral authority. Nelson Mandela's path reflected extraordinary personal choice—but also political vision, strategic judgment, and a collective struggle far larger than one man. Still, one element stands out: He refused to let the prison author the meaning of his life. The facts of those 27 years never changed. What they meant—for him, and for a nation—was still, in part, his to decide.

Leaving With More Questions

I cannot teach you what your past means. Nobody can: The meaning of your past cannot be assigned to you by someone else. It can only be authored by you. All I can do is what my mentor did to me in front of that elevator: hand you a confusion worth keeping.

So here it is once more. Your history is fixed. Its meaning is not. The past writes the first draft of your story—but you hold the pen for every revision, for as long as you live.

If you walked into this post with three questions and are leaving with 10, then—by the only measure my mentor ever gave me—we have done our job, you and I.

Childhood adversity and abuse are difficult topics. If this post has stirred painful memories, support is available. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory. In the United States, you can call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or you can reach the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4453; outside the United States, findahelpline.com lists local services.

item.title: How to Get the Most Out of Your Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

How to Get the Most Out of Your Therapy

You’re a consumer paying for a service, so don’t just take what you get.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • To get the most out of therapy, it's important to be both open and proactive.
  • All too often, clients worry about being judged or are unsure what is and is not important to talk about.
  • The key is to be clear about your expectations and goals, do research, and be assertive in sessions.
Source: newleafmentalhealth/pixabay

At a social event a few years ago, I met a fellow who, as we got to know each other, mentioned that he had been in therapy for a couple of years. He felt his wife had been emotionally pulling back, that they were living parallel lives, and that he was using therapy to help him navigate and hopefully improve the relationship. He then admitted he had had an affair, which his wife had discovered, and acknowledged that this betrayal was undoubtedly fueling his wife’s behavior. Though he was openly telling me, a relative stranger, all this, he said he had never mentioned the affair to his therapist.

I’ve met others who have also been in therapy for years with the same therapist and come to see me professionally because they feel the therapy has stalled over the past year or so. While they enjoy their weekly sessions and look forward to seeing their therapist, they feel they aren’t learning anything new or actively working on their problems. They’re treading water, and both are on autopilot.

What these situations have in common is that they’re not getting the most out of their therapy. Here are the common dynamics driving each situation:

Not speaking up.

We could imagine a few reasons someone might not be self-disclosing with their therapist:

  • Shame and judgment. You may feel ashamed of your behaviors, feelings, or thoughts and anticipate judgment, especially if you tend to be self-critical or have experienced criticism from significant others.
  • Not understanding what is important. As a client, you’re trying to adapt to your therapist’s orientation and style. You only learn what is important to talk about based on the questions they ask. If the fellow’s therapist never asked about any history of affairs, he might assume it was not necessary to share that information. Similarly, if a cognitive-behavioral therapist asks about your thoughts and feelings in a specific situation rather than family history, you may assume that discussing any childhood trauma is not necessarily important.
  • Not engaged. Finally, you may withhold important information because you’re trying to appease someone else who believes you need therapy. You’re not engaged, being passive, simply coasting and letting the therapist set the pace and focus.

Going on autopilot

Some clients need longer-term, supportive therapy that focuses less on working through problems and developing skills and instead emphasizes accountability and maintenance; clients who, for example, benefit from checking in with someone to help them stay on their medication, or who are isolated and need someone to help prevent the buildup of stress. But that is different from situations where it’s not about providing ongoing support, but rather both the therapist and client have downshifted the therapy from focusing on change to maintaining the comfortable relationship. To avoid this, a reputable therapist will regularly check in with you to see whether you’re still getting what you need.

If you want to get the most out of your therapy, what should you do? Here are some suggestions:

Decide what your #1 goal is

Therapy is a means to an end: What is your end? What are you hoping to get out of therapy? Skills for managing a relationship better; unraveling trauma from your past that is affecting your present; or reducing depression or anxiety?

Decide on any preferences you have for the process

Do you prefer to see a woman or a man? Do you feel you could benefit from exploring your past, or would you rather focus on the here and now and learn specific skills? Can you afford long-term therapy? If you’ve been in therapy before, what did you like or dislike about it? If you’ve never been in therapy, you likely still have some expectations about how it might best help you.

Do your research

Once you’ve clarified your goals and preferences, it’s time to start searching. Use one or more online therapist directories to review profiles, or check Reddit forums for feedback on people’s experiences. Look for therapists who specialize in your issue and whose clinical model aligns with your expectations. If you’re comfortable with remote sessions, you can generally see anyone licensed in your state.

Interview the therapist

Once you’ve identified one or two potential candidates, contact them to ask questions. Some therapists are comfortable with short phone calls; others prefer to answer questions by email; some want you to come in for a trial session to see if it’s a good fit. Decide what you’re comfortable with, ask what they’re willing to do as a starting point, have specific questions ready, state your goals clearly, and if you’re exploring options, let them know. Think of the process as similar to buying a car, gathering the information you need to make an informed decision.

Be proactive

Yes, you’re starting a new relationship with a stranger, and it takes time to feel safe enough to be fully open. That said, be proactive and hit the ground running. Decide before your session what you want to talk about and what you want to get out of it that day. If you don’t understand why the therapist is focusing on a particular line of inquiry, ask. If you are bothered by something your therapist said, try to find the courage to share your feedback with them.

And if, after, say, five sessions, you’re still not comfortable opening up, or the therapist’s style and focus don’t seem like a good fit, speak up to see whether something about the process needs to be tweaked, or terminate and find another.

Like working with any professional, there is often a perceived power imbalance. It’s easy to feel intimidated, which can lead you to follow their lead and hold back on asking questions or giving feedback. But keep in mind that you are, in fact, a consumer paying for a service. Step up, speak up, and get what you need.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Can Learning a Language Keep Your Brain Young?
item.description:
Cognition

Can Learning a Language Keep Your Brain Young?

What learning another language can do for your aging brain.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Learning another language is one of the brain's most demanding workouts.
  • Research suggests bilingualism may delay the onset of dementia symptoms.
  • Speaking another language strengthens both cognition and social connection.

Can you exercise your brain the way you exercise your body? The answer appears to be yes, and one of the most effective workouts may be learning another language.

As we age, many of us look for ways to stay mentally sharp. We tackle crossword puzzles, download brain-training apps, and take up new hobbies in the hope of preserving our memory and thinking skills. Increasingly, researchers are pointing to another activity that challenges the brain in a particularly powerful way: learning a new language.

Unlike many pastimes that exercise a single mental skill, language learning engages almost every major cognitive system at once. It calls on memory, attention, problem-solving, pattern recognition, and mental flexibility. Every conversation is a rapid-fire exercise in selecting words, applying grammar, suppressing competing alternatives, and interpreting meaning in real time. Few everyday activities ask quite so much of the brain.

Building a More Resilient Brain

One reason scientists are fascinated by bilingualism is its relationship with cognitive reserve, which is the brain's ability to cope with age-related changes or neurological damage while continuing to function effectively.

Think of cognitive reserve as an alternative route through a busy city. If one road is blocked, a well-connected network offers plenty of other ways to reach the destination. Likewise, a brain with greater cognitive reserve may be better able to compensate for damage before symptoms become obvious.

Research suggests that speaking more than one language may help build this reserve (Stollznow, 2026). Some studies have found that bilingual people may experience the symptoms of dementia several years later than their monolingual peers. Although learning another language is certainly not a guarantee against Alzheimer's disease or other forms of dementia, it appears to be one of several lifestyle habits that may help support healthier cognitive aging.

How Language Changes the Brain

Language learning doesn't simply fill our minds with new vocabulary; it appears to change the brain itself.

Our brains are made up of neurons and the dense web of connections between them. Studies have shown that people who grow up bilingual often have greater gray matter density in regions associated with attention, memory, and executive function (Korenar et al., 2023). Bilingualism has also been linked to stronger white matter, the network of nerve fibers that allows different parts of the brain to communicate efficiently. Better-connected brain networks are associated with faster information processing and stronger cognitive performance.

The encouraging news is that these benefits are not limited to people who learned two languages in childhood. Adults also form new neural pathways as they master unfamiliar sounds, grammar, and vocabulary (Pliatsikas, 2020). Each new word and grammatical pattern becomes another connection within an ever-expanding network. With repeated use, those pathways become more efficient, allowing the brain to process information with increasing ease.

More Than Mental Exercise

The cognitive benefits of language learning extend well beyond memory. Studies have linked learning another language with improvements in concentration, working memory, and executive function, the mental skills that allow us to plan, adapt, focus attention, and solve problems (Bialystok, 2017). Some research has even found that language learners perform better in subjects such as mathematics and science, suggesting that the benefits can transfer beyond language itself.

Just as importantly, every language offers a different way of organizing experience. Learning another language means encountering new ways of expressing emotions, relationships, humor, and identity. In doing so, we often become more open to perspectives other than our own. Research has linked language learning with greater empathy, cultural awareness, and cognitive flexibility, qualities that enrich our relationships as much as our intellect.

No single activity can promise a healthy brain forever. Genetics, education, physical activity, sleep, diet, and social connection all play important roles. But learning another language stands out because it combines many of these protective ingredients into a single pursuit. It challenges the mind, rewards curiosity, fosters human connection, and may even help build a brain that's better prepared for the years ahead.

That's a compelling reason to keep learning, one conversation at a time.

Read about this topic and more in Karen Stollznow’s new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language.

item.title: “We’re Staying Together for the Kids"
item.description:
Family Dynamics

“We’re Staying Together for the Kids"

What children actually experience in chronically tense homes.

Posted August 6, 2026

There is a particular kind of family that, from the outside, appears intact and perfect. Both parents are present. Routines are maintained. The children go to school, attend activities, and move through their days with a structure that looks, at least superficially, stable.

Inside the home, the atmosphere tells a different story: Conversations are brief. Eye contact between parents is limited or edged with irritation. Tension is constant. At times, it escalates into a conflict that never quite resolves.

Children growing up in these homes notice tone, posture, silence, and the timing of a sigh. They learn when to speak, when to stay quiet, when to make themselves small, and when to try to shift the energy.

Parents in such scenarios may say with sincerity, “We are staying together for the kids.” From a systemic perspective, this is precisely where the question needs to be reconsidered—because children are not shaped by whether a family stays together, but by the emotional system in which they grow up.

The promise of stability

The decision to stay in a marriage for the children is usually rooted in care, not neglect. Parents worry about disrupting routines, splitting time between households, introducing financial strain, or exposing children to the uncertainty of divorce. Many carry their own histories of loss or instability and want to prevent their children from experiencing something similar.

Research complicates this assumption, as studies show that the presence of two parents in the same household does not predict child well-being. What does is the quality of the emotional climate between those parents (Amato, 2010; Kelly & Emery, 2003).

Children in emotionally stable homes tend to do well regardless of family structure. Those exposed to chronic interparental conflict, emotional withdrawal, or persistent tension are at greater risk for anxiety, depression, behavioral difficulties, and relational problems later in life (Cummings & Davies, 2010).

A systemic lens on what children absorb

From a systemic perspective, children are not passive observers of their parents’ relationship. They are active participants in a relational field that is continuously organizing around patterns of connection, disconnection, tension, and repair. They do not simply witness these dynamics; they adapt to them.

One of the most robust findings in this area comes from Emotional Security Theory, which suggests that children use the relationship between their caregivers as a primary indicator of safety (Cummings & Davies, 2010). When that relationship is marked by chronic tension, unresolved conflict, or emotional distance, children’s sense of security becomes destabilized.

Importantly, this does not require overt hostility. Even in homes where conflict is muted or avoided, the absence of warmth and connection can create an environment that feels unpredictable or emotionally unsafe. Children organize around this in ways that are often invisible to the adults in the system.

Chronic emotional vigilance

In chronically tense homes, children become highly attuned to shifts in the emotional climate. They monitor tone of voice, facial expressions, and patterns of interaction. They anticipate conflict before it happens and adjust their own behavior in response. This kind of vigilance is adaptive in the short term, but over time, it comes at a cost. Sustained activation of this kind is associated with increased anxiety, difficulty concentrating, sleep disturbances, and heightened physiological stress responses. The result is a nervous system that learns to stay alert.

Learning what relationships are

Children develop their understanding of relationships through repeated exposure. In families with disconnected or conflictual marriages, they may come to understand that closeness involves distance, conflict leads to escalation or withdrawal, and emotional needs are either unmet or burdensome. These patterns contribute to the development of internal working models that shape how they approach relationships later in life.

Loyalty to one parent can feel like betrayal of the other. Attending to their own needs can feel like abandoning the family. Over time, this can lead to chronic guilt, difficulty setting boundaries, and a sense of responsibility for other people’s emotional states.

Conflict without repair

All relationships involve conflict. What matters for children is not the presence of conflict, but the presence of repair. Gottman and Gottman’s (2026) research on relational conflict highlights patterns such as criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling as particularly damaging when they become chronic within a relationship. Their work also demonstrates that relationships marked by persistent hostility, emotional withdrawal, and unresolved conflict are associated with poorer relational and emotional outcomes not only for couples themselves, but for the children growing up within these emotional environments.

Without exposure to genuine repair, children may come to experience conflict as either dangerous or final. They may struggle to tolerate disagreement or to trust that relationships can withstand strain. Their own future relationships may follow similar patterns or become organized around fear of conflict, emotional withdrawal, instability, or chronic insecurity.

The illusion of stability

From the outside, a family that remains together may seem stable. From within a systemic lens, stability requires more than continuity of structure. It requires a level of emotional regulation, predictability, and responsiveness that allows members of the system to feel secure. When a marriage is chronically tense, emotionally depleted, or marked by unresolved conflict, what is maintained is not stability, but a kind of frozen equilibrium. Children adapt to this, often in ways that appear functional. For example, they may succeed academically, behave appropriately, and avoid drawing attention to the underlying dynamics.

Rethinking the question

For many parents, the decision to stay together is framed as a choice between preserving the family or disrupting it. A more useful question, from a systemic perspective, is: In what emotional system are children growing up? Are they experiencing safety, warmth, and repair, even in the presence of imperfection? Or are they adapting to chronic tension, emotional distance, and unresolved conflict?

For many couples, these decisions also exist within larger cultural, religious, economic, and intergenerational systems that shape beliefs about marriage, sacrifice, parenting, divorce, gender roles, and family obligation.

Clinical implications

For couple therapists, this dynamic shows up frequently. Couples present with the explicit goal of staying together for the children, while describing patterns of interaction that are persistently tense, disconnected, or conflictual. The work in these cases is not to challenge the decision to stay or to leave but to bring the system into view.

This includes helping couples understand how children experience the relational field, identifying patterns of triangulation or parentification, and understanding the impact of chronic hypervigilance in children adapting to ongoing parental tension. It also involves naming, carefully and without judgment, when the current structure is not functioning as protection.

Creating space for these conversations and helping couples move toward greater discernment is often an important part of protecting the emotional well-being of the children within the system.

What matters is not whether parents remain together at all costs. It is whether the system they create allows the child to develop without having to organize themselves around chronic relational stress and adopt hypervigilance around persistent parental discord.

A systemic perspective invites families to examine these dynamics honestly and compassionately, while recognizing that children are shaped less by the structure itself than by the emotional climate in which they grow up.

Bahareh Sahebi, PsyD, LMFT

Bahareh Sahebi, PsyD, LMFT, is a clinical psychologist and licensed marriage and family therapist in the metropolitan Chicago area. Her clinical work is grounded in Integrative Systemic Therapy, with a focus on the clinical presentation of trauma, differentiation, and multigenerational transmission processes.

item.title: Why Walk and Talk Therapy Matters More in the Age of AI
item.description:
Therapeutic Alliance

Why Walk and Talk Therapy Matters More in the Age of AI

Healing requires more than insights. It happens through lived experiences.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Information alone can not create lasting change.
  • Relational therapy with a human provides an experience that AI cannot replicate.
  • Walk and talk therapy supports mental health experientially.
  • Nature and movement support mindfulness and regulation.
Source: Liza Summer / Pexels

Co-authored by Aimee Frazier and Glenn Seiver

Artificial intelligence may become the most significant source of psychological information the world has ever known. As millions of people now turn to AI for a deeper understanding of their psychological issues, access to mental health information no longer depends solely on a therapist. It is ironic that AI makes the human aspects of therapy even more valuable, because although AI can offer information, therapists have always known that information by itself is not enough to achieve lasting healing. Healing is experiential, not informational.

Psychological changes that improve mental health require integrating information, and experiential and relational shifts that reshape someone’s experience of life. AI cannot replace the therapeutic relationship or the benefits that come with physical movement and time in nature.

AI Can Explain Attachment. Therapy Provides a Secure Relationship.

Healing occurs through a therapeutic relationship built on trust, empathy, and understanding. While AI can simulate conversation, it cannot replace the human connection that develops between therapist and client. Interpersonal neurobiology suggests that the human mind develops and heals within human relationships, making connection a fundamental ingredient of psychological well-being. Humans are highly tuned in to one another, able to pick up on facial expressions, movement, posture, and nonverbal cues. Often, in the presence of a trusted therapist, the nervous system has an opportunity to relax through a process known as co-regulation—a lived experience of relational safety that cannot be replicated by information.

AI Can Recommend Exercise for Mental Health. Walk and Talk Therapy Is the Experience of It.

Rather than reading the suggestion to "go for a walk," many clients are already engaging in one of the very behaviors known to improve mood and emotional regulation. Therapy and behavior activation occur simultaneously. The American Psychological Association notes that physical activity has significant positive effects on mood and emotional well-being, while research published in The Lancet Psychiatry found that individuals who exercise regularly report substantially fewer days of poor mental health than those who do not (Chekroud et al., 2018). During walk and talk therapy, these physiological benefits occur simultaneously with therapeutic conversation. Clients are not simply talking about coping; they are actively engaging in behaviors that naturally support their mental health.

AI Can Describe Mindfulness. Nature Invites Them Into It.

Nature is an active part of the therapeutic experience in walk and talk sessions. Unlike an office with four walls, the outdoor environment is restorative and dynamic: One week may include bright sunshine reflecting off a lake. Another may involve crisp autumn leaves, gentle snowfall, or the calming sound of rain falling on the tree canopy above.

These sensory-rich environments naturally encourage mindfulness by anchoring awareness in the present moment through the five senses—noticing sights, smells, sensations of the wind and sun on the skin, sounds, and taste. This reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression by bringing awareness to the here and now, rather than drifting toward concerns for the future or ruminations about the past. Research suggests that spending time in natural environments can lower stress, improve mood, and restore attention (Bratman et al., 2019).

Over time, the trail itself can become a resource. Clients often return to the same paths outside of therapy, finding that places they have come to associate with their growth continue to support them by offering space to process and feel grounded. Environmental psychology refers to these emotional bonds with places as place attachment: Places that hold significant meaning and offer a sense of safety and emotional relief.

AI Can Explain Shame and Trauma Reactions. Compassionate Witnessing Can Change Them.

One of our most fundamental human needs is to be seen, understood, and met with compassion by those around us. For many people who experienced childhood neglect, abuse, or other developmental trauma, those experiences were painfully absent. Instead, trauma survivors often learned to expect rejection, abandonment, criticism, or neglect, leaving them with a sense of shame or the deeply held belief that they are somehow fundamentally flawed.

Recovering from complex trauma happens through repeated, corrective experiences of relational safety, acceptance, and care. Over time, this re-shapes interpersonal expectations and beliefs about the self. Walk and talk therapy and the side-by-side relational dynamic often make it easier for clients to share painful emotions and experiences, opening the door for compassionate responses from the therapist that can facilitate these corrective emotional and relational experiences. AI can explain trauma reactions and reflect back the internal experiences associated with trauma, but it cannot provide the experience of a compassionate human presence that helps rewrite internal templates.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of explaining the human mind, the greatest value of therapy will not be in providing more information to clients, but in guiding experiential transformations from one human to another.

Source: Dan Paterno

Glenn Sevier, LCSW, PEL, is a Chicago-based psychotherapist and the founder of Walk-N-Talk Therapy, an innovative approach that combines movement, nature, and counseling. With more than 36 years of experience, Glenn helps individuals create meaningful, lasting changes in their lives. Additional information about Glenn’s clinical services is available on LinkedIn and Psychology Today. His work has been featured by leading media outlets, including NBC News, ABC News, and the Chicago Tribune.
